design_detail: Secondary analysis of a single-arm, open-label feasibility trial (the Bristol Imperial MDMA in Alcoholism study, BIMA; ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04158778, phase 1; EudraCT 2016-002547-42 per the registry) in 14 adults with alcohol use disorder who had recently completed detoxification, all given an eight-week course of ten psychotherapy sessions of which sessions 3 and 7 included MDMA. The safety and tolerability results were published earlier (Sessa et al., 2021, J Psychopharmacol; not read here, not free). This paper reports a binomial test and a Bayesian re-expression of one binary outcome (a reduction of two WHO drinking risk levels from baseline to 3 months after treatment) and pre–post changes in self-reported craving, quality of life, sleep, self-compassion and empathy at 3 months. Sponsor Imperial College London; funded by the Alexander Mosley Charitable Trust. The schema has no single-arm-trial design; 'case-series' is the closest (an uncontrolled before–after study of one treated group), and the card uses ROBINS-I as the batch brief directs for non-randomized intervention studies.
can_establish: What happened to self-reported drinking risk levels, craving, sleep, quality of life, self-compassion and empathy over about five months in 14 detoxified adults with alcohol use disorder who received an eight-week psychotherapy course including two MDMA sessions, and how often a two-level fall in WHO drinking risk was seen in this group.
cannot_establish: Whether MDMA, the psychotherapy, the preceding detoxification, the natural course after detoxification, regression to the mean or expectation produced any of these changes (there is no comparison group and no blinding); whether the changes last beyond 3 months (the registered 6- and 9-month outcomes are not reported here); or anything about people the study excluded (people taking antidepressants who were unwilling to stop, serious suicide risk, psychotic or personality disorders, cardiovascular or severe liver disease, regular ecstasy use, other drug dependence) or about non-White populations.

sample.recruitment: Not described in this paper, which refers to Sessa et al. (2021) for full details (Materials and methods › Participants; Procedure, 1st paragraph). The registry describes detoxified patients with alcohol use disorder at a Bristol and Imperial study (registry record, Identification; Eligibility).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Registry: primary DSM-5 diagnosis of alcohol use disorder; successful alcohol detoxification (no longer drinking); age 18 to 65; a supportive significant other who could accompany the participant or help collect follow-up data; English proficiency. Excluded: lack of capacity; psychotic disorder, bipolar I or personality disorder; serious suicide risk (C-SSRS and clinical judgement); cardiac disease, hypertension, stroke, severe liver disease, epilepsy, malignant hyperthermia; regular ecstasy use (for example more than five times in five years or at least twice in the 6 months before the study); medicines that inhibit CYP2D6 or interact with MDMA, including MAO inhibitors, several SSRIs and regular benzodiazepines, unless stopped for the 8-week course; regular use of or dependence on other drugs; pregnancy or breast-feeding (registry record, Eligibility). The paper's own summary of the criteria (antidepressants unless titrated off, serious suicide risk, psychotic or personality disorders, cardiovascular and severe liver disease) agrees (Discussion › Limitations, 2nd paragraph). The paper's own sentence on age is corrupted in the PMC text (reporting issues).
sample.demographics: 8 men and 6 women; mean age 48 years; all White British (Results › Demographics, 1st paragraph). Other characteristics, including baseline drinking, are only in Sessa et al. (2021), not read.
sample.attrition: The abstract says all 14 completed the eight-week course (Abstract › Methods). The WHO risk-level analysis uses all 14 (Table 1); the questionnaire analyses at 3 months use 11 to 14 participants (Fig. 2 and Fig. 3 legends) with no account of the missing data.
sample.selection_effects: People who had already succeeded in detoxification, had a supportive significant other and were willing to take MDMA in a research setting; regular ecstasy use, other drug dependence and much psychiatric and physical comorbidity excluded; all White British. Fourteen of an estimated 20 in the registry. Expectations of benefit were probably high and were not measured.

exposure.measurement: Assigned treatment, given to everyone: an eight-week recovery-based therapy course of ten psychotherapy sessions using motivational interviewing and third-wave cognitive-behavioural elements, with MDMA in sessions 3 and 7 and psychotherapy alone in the other sessions; participants stayed overnight in the treatment centre after each MDMA session (Materials and methods › Procedure, 2nd paragraph; Discussion › Future directions, 1st and 2nd paragraphs). Good Manufacturing Practice MDMA from Sterling Pharmaceuticals, formulated into capsules by the Pharmacy Manufacturing Unit at Guy's and St Thomas' NHS Foundation Trust (Materials and methods › Approvals and drug source, 1st paragraph).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions as printed: by mouth in two sessions (3 and 7) of the eight-week course, an initial dose of 125 mg followed by a booster of 62.5 mg; capsules of 62.5 mg (Materials and methods › Procedure, 2nd paragraph; Approvals and drug source, 1st paragraph). How many participants took the booster is reported only in Sessa et al. (2021).
exposure.polysubstance: Regular use of or dependence on other drugs (benzodiazepines, synthetic cannabinoids, cocaine, heroin) and regular ecstasy use were exclusion criteria (registry record, Eligibility). The registry says illicit drug use and any recreational MDMA use after the trial would be recorded; neither is reported in this paper.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Participants had completed alcohol detoxification before the course. Drinking afterwards was measured by Timeline Followback, a self-report interview; no biological verification is reported (Materials and methods › WHO risk drinking level, 1st paragraph).

comparison.controls: None. Each participant's 3-month values are compared with their own baseline. The paper does not state which period the baseline drinking covers; the registry describes the drinking comparison as pre-detoxification (screening) levels against later visits (registry record, Outcome Measures, 'Change in Drinking behaviour').
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable as such; without a comparison group the natural course after detoxification, the psychotherapy itself, regression to the mean (people enrolled at a low point) and expectation are all uncontrolled.

outcomes.instruments: Timeline Followback (TLFB), alcohol units converted to WHO drinking risk levels; Penn Alcohol Craving Scale (PACS; five items scored 0 to 6); Obsessive Compulsive Drinking Scale (OCDS; 14 items, obsessive and compulsive subscales); SF-36 (eight domains scored 0 to 100, plus reported change in health); four items derived from the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index combined into one sleep-disturbance score; Self-Compassion Scale (26 items); Interpersonal Reactivity Index (IRI; four 7-item subscales) (Materials and methods › WHO risk drinking level; PROMs).
outcomes.validity_norms: Standard validated questionnaires, except the sleep score, which uses four items derived from the PSQI rather than the PSQI itself (Materials and methods › PROMs › Sleep). The two-level reduction in WHO risk drinking levels is presented as an endpoint accepted by the EMA as an intermediate harm-reduction endpoint and in the FDA's outcome-assessment qualification process, not yet fully qualified (Introduction, 3rd paragraph; Discussion, 2nd paragraph).
outcomes.operationalization: Treatment success: a reduction of two WHO drinking risk levels from baseline to 3 months after treatment, from TLFB units (Materials and methods › WHO risk drinking level). The questionnaires: change from baseline to 3 months.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Bonferroni correction within questionnaires that have several subscales (OCDS, SF-36, IRI); none across questionnaires. Editors' count of 19 tests in the text: the WHO risk-level outcome, PACS total, two OCDS subscales, eight SF-36 domains and the reported-change item, the sleep score, the Self-Compassion Scale total and four IRI subscales. The authors acknowledge possible Type I error inflation and call the findings hypothesis-generating (Materials and methods › Data analysis, 3rd paragraph; Discussion › Limitations, 1st paragraph).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: None: open-label; all outcomes self-reported or, for the TLFB, collected by the study team, with participants and staff aware of the treatment.

analysis.effect_sizes: WHO risk level: 9 of 14 achieved a two-level reduction at 3 months; binomial test against 50%, proportion .64, P = .423, 95% CI 0.35 to 0.87; mean posterior success rate 0.63 (credible interval 0.40 to 0.85) with a flat Beta(1,1) prior and 0.55 (0.33 to 0.77) with a Beta(1,3) prior called sceptical (Results › Bayesian analysis…, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 1). Editors' check: two-sided exact binomial P = 0.424 and Clopper–Pearson interval 0.351 to 0.872; posteriors Beta(10,6), mean 0.625, highest-density interval 0.40 to 0.85, and Beta(10,8), mean 0.556, 0.33 to 0.77 (the printed intervals match highest-density intervals). Questionnaires, 3 months vs baseline (Wilcoxon signed-rank, differences with 95% CI and rank-biserial r): PACS 5.50 (0.5 to 13), P = .031, r .781; OCDS obsessive 5.00 (2.00 to 8.50), P = .006, r .868, compulsive 5.00 (1.00 to 9.00), P = .021, r .769; sleep score 2.00 (7.54e-6 to 3.00), P = .041, r .648; Self-Compassion Scale 12.1 (9.09 to 14.4), P < .001, r 1.00; IRI personal distress 0.5 (0.143 to 0.929), P = .009, r .945; SF-36 subscales not significant after correction (Results, subsections). Within-group changes only; no between-group effect exists.
analysis.preregistration_detail: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04158778 was first submitted on 31 January 2019 and first posted on 12 November 2019, after the study's actual start (18 April 2018): retrospective registration (the EudraCT number 2016-002547-42 is listed but that register was not read). Registered primary outcome: safety and tolerability (completion of the course, acceptance of the booster dose, adverse events). Registered secondary outcomes include change in drinking behaviour by TLFB (pre-detoxification screening levels against session 10 and 3, 6 and 9 months), SF-36, PSQI, SIP, GAD-7, PHQ-9, IRI, Self-Compassion Scale, PACS, OCDS, prescribed medication use and recreational MDMA use, each at 3, 6 and 9 months. The two-level WHO risk-level endpoint and the Bayesian analysis are not registered outcomes; the sleep measure reported is four PSQI-derived items rather than the PSQI; no results are posted (registry record, read through the ClinicalTrials.gov API v2 on 2026-10-17).
analysis.selective_reporting: Only the 3-month time point is reported for registered outcomes that were planned at 3, 6 and 9 months; SIP, GAD-7, PHQ-9, prescribed medication use and recreational MDMA use are not reported here (anxiety and depression results are said to be in Sessa et al., 2021); the full statistics for the questionnaires are only in a supplementary Word file (Tables S1 to S12), not read because it is a download; Figs 2 and 3 are images and no values were extracted from them.
analysis.power: No power calculation; a feasibility sample of 14 (registry estimate 20). The authors call the sample small and the analysis exploratory (Discussion › Limitations, 1st paragraph).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In one uncontrolled group of 14 detoxified adults with alcohol use disorder, 9 had drinking at least two WHO risk levels lower 3 months after an eight-week psychotherapy course with two MDMA sessions than at baseline, which the registry describes as drinking before detoxification; the Bayesian analysis restates 9 of 14 as a posterior success rate of 0.55 to 0.63 depending on the prior and adds no comparison. Self-reported craving, a four-item sleep score, self-compassion and one empathy subscale improved between baseline and 3 months in the 11 to 14 people with data; quality-of-life subscales did not survive correction. None of these changes can be attributed to MDMA.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract presents the Bayesian analysis as a useful harm-reduction interpretation of drinking (Abstract › Conclusions). The Discussion compares the 55% to 63% success rate with 68% from secondary analyses of the COMBINE study and Project MATCH and says the results suggest MDMA-assisted psychotherapy "may produce clinically meaningful reductions in alcohol consumption" comparable with established treatments (Discussion, 2nd paragraph): a comparison across studies with different populations, baselines and treatments, made from a single-arm study. It says MDMA's acute prosocial effects "appear to persist" because self-compassion and personal distress improved (Discussion, 5th paragraph), a causal reading of pre–post change without a control. The Limitations call the findings hypothesis-generating and ask for randomized placebo-controlled trials, measurement of unblinding and expectancy, and long-term follow-up (Discussion › Limitations, 1st and 2nd paragraphs).

timeline.event: Sessa et al., J Psychopharmacol: the safety and tolerability report of the same 14 participants, with drinking and mood outcomes to 9 months (cited by this paper; not read here because it is not free; DOI 10.1177/0269881121991792).
This paper: Bayesian re-expression of the two-level WHO risk-level outcome at 3 months (9 of 14) and 3-month questionnaire changes.

replication.where_it_stands: One open-label study of 14 people, reported twice by the same group. No randomized or otherwise controlled trial of MDMA-assisted therapy in alcohol use disorder was among the sources read; the project's evidence map lists protocols of two trials in people with both PTSD and alcohol use disorder (Eaton et al., 2024; Morley et al., 2026), not read here.

funding.funder: The Alexander Mosley Charitable Trust funded the entire clinical trial (Funding). Sponsor: Imperial College London (Materials and methods › Approvals and drug source, 1st paragraph; Ethics statement). The Methods state that Awakn Life Sciences Corporation has exclusive rights to the data from 'the Phase 2b' (Approvals and drug source, 1st paragraph).
funding.declared_conflicts: As printed: HT was a Senior Research Officer at Drug Science, collaborating with industry partners developing medical psychedelics, and was seconded to Awakn Life Sciences, positions no longer held at submission; DJN is Chief Scientific Officer of Awakn Life Sciences; CJAM was seconded to Awakn Life Sciences and the University of Exeter has licensed intellectual property from her work to Awakn; 'BS, LH, SO, CD, SW, BS' declare no conflicts (Conflict of interest).
funding.affiliations_note: Seven of nine authors are at Imperial College London; Ben Sessa is listed as an independent consultant (Contributor Information). A company in which the senior author is Chief Scientific Officer holds exclusive data rights, and the first author was seconded to it. Data available on reasonable request from the first author (Data availability).

what_would_settle_it: A preregistered randomized trial in adults with alcohol use disorder, after detoxification, comparing the same psychotherapy with MDMA against an active comparator, with the drinking baseline taken after detoxification, drinking verified biologically (for example phosphatidylethanol), blinding and expectancy measured, independent outcome assessors, and follow-up for at least 12 months.

domains.note: No comparison group. The drinking outcome is compared with a baseline that the registry places before detoxification, so the change mixes detoxification, the psychotherapy, the natural course after detoxification and regression to the mean with any effect of MDMA; none of these can be separated in a single-arm design.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of participants into the study
domains.note: Participants entered after successful detoxification and had to have a supportive significant other; selection on early success could favour good outcomes, though it bears more on who the results apply to than on the pre–post change itself.
Everyone received the same protocolized course with two MDMA sessions.

domains.domain: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
domains.note: Co-interventions between the end of the course and 3 months (other alcohol treatment, medicines, mutual-help groups) are not reported in this paper; booster acceptance is only in Sessa et al. (2021).
Questionnaire analyses at 3 months use 11 to 14 of 14 participants without any account of who was missing or why; how missing TLFB data were handled for the WHO risk-level outcome is not stated.
All outcomes are self-reported (TLFB interview and questionnaires) by participants who knew they had received MDMA, collected by the unblinded study team, with no biological verification of drinking.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
domains.note: Retrospective registration; the two-level WHO risk-level endpoint and the Bayesian analysis are not registered; registered 6- and 9-month results and several registered measures are not reported; the sleep measure differs from the registered PSQI.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: As evidence about the effect of MDMA-assisted therapy, the study is at critical risk of bias because it has no comparison group and its drinking baseline appears to precede detoxification (registry), so the before–after change cannot be attributed to the intervention, still less to MDMA. Missing questionnaire data without explanation, self-reported unblinded outcomes and an unregistered endpoint add serious concerns. The paper can be cited for what was observed in this small open-label group (9 of 14 with a two-level fall in WHO drinking risk at 3 months; changes in self-reported craving, sleep and self-compassion) and for the fact that no controlled evidence exists; it cannot be cited for efficacy, for comparison with standard treatments, or for durability.

key_findings.finding: Fourteen participants with alcohol use disorder who had recently been detoxified completed an eight-week course of ten psychotherapy sessions, two of them with MDMA; 8 men and 6 women, mean age 48, all White British.
Two-level reduction in WHO drinking risk from baseline to 3 months after treatment: 9 of 14 participants; binomial test against an expected 50%, proportion .64, P = .423, 95% CI 0.35 to 0.87.
key_findings.locator: Results › Bayesian analysis of World Health Organization drinking risk level at 3 months follow-up, 1st paragraph; Table 1
key_findings.note: Editors' check: exact two-sided P = 0.424; Clopper–Pearson 95% CI 0.351 to 0.872.

key_findings.finding: Bayesian analysis of the same 9 of 14: mean posterior success rate 0.63 (credible interval 0.40 to 0.85) with a flat Beta(1,1) prior and 0.55 (0.33 to 0.77) with a Beta(1,3) prior, described as sceptical, with a mean of 25% chosen from typical placebo response rates of 25% to 40% in mental health trials.
key_findings.locator: Table 1; Results › Bayesian analysis of World Health Organization drinking risk level at 3 months follow-up, 2nd paragraph; Materials and methods › Data analysis, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: Editors' check: posteriors Beta(10,6), mean 0.625, 95% highest-density interval 0.40 to 0.85, and Beta(10,8), mean 0.556 (printed 0.55), 0.33 to 0.77. The posterior is an estimate of the success rate in this single group; it involves no comparison.

key_findings.finding: Craving at 3 months vs baseline (n = 13): PACS total difference 5.50 (95% CI 0.5 to 13), P = .031, rank-biserial r .781; OCDS obsessive subscale 5.00 (2.00 to 8.50), P = .006, r .868; OCDS compulsive subscale 5.00 (1.00 to 9.00), P = .021, r .769.
key_findings.locator: Results › Drinking behavior at 3 months follow-up, 1st paragraph; Fig. 2 legend

key_findings.finding: Quality of life (SF-36, n = 11): energy/fatigue, emotional well-being, social functioning, pain, general health and reported change in health rose nominally at 3 months, but no subscale remained significant after Bonferroni correction.
key_findings.locator: Results › Quality of life, sleep, well-being, and psychosocial functioning measures › Quality of life, 1st paragraph; Fig. 3 legend

key_findings.finding: Sleep (four PSQI-derived items, n = 14): difference 2.00 (95% CI 7.54e-6 to 3.00), P = .041, r .648, lower scores meaning less disturbance.
key_findings.locator: Results › Quality of life, sleep, well-being, and psychosocial functioning measures › Sleep, 1st paragraph; Materials and methods › PROMs › Sleep; Fig. 3 legend

key_findings.finding: Self-Compassion Scale total (n = 13): increase of 12.1 (95% CI 9.09 to 14.4), P < .001, r 1.00; IRI (n = 12): only the personal distress subscale changed, falling by 0.5 (0.143 to 0.929), P = .009, r .945.
key_findings.locator: Results › Quality of life, sleep, well-being, and psychosocial functioning measures › Self-compassion, 1st paragraph; › Empathy, 1st paragraph; Fig. 3 legend

key_findings.finding: Analysis: Wilcoxon matched-pairs signed-rank tests with 95% CIs around the differences; Bonferroni correction only within questionnaires with several subscales; the authors acknowledge possible Type I error inflation, call the findings hypothesis-generating rather than evidence of efficacy, and say larger randomized placebo-controlled trials, measurement of unblinding and expectancy, and long-term follow-up are needed.
key_findings.locator: Materials and methods › Data analysis, 3rd paragraph; Discussion › Limitations, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: The Discussion compares the 55% to 63% success rate with the 68% of patients reaching a two-level WHO risk reduction at the end of treatment in secondary analyses of the COMBINE study and Project MATCH, calling the results comparable with established treatments.

Registry: NCT04158778 (BIMA), single-group open-label, phase 1, estimated enrollment 20; actual start 18 April 2018, first submitted 31 January 2019, first posted 12 November 2019; primary outcome safety and tolerability; secondary outcomes include change in drinking by TLFB from pre-detoxification (screening) levels to session 10 and 3, 6 and 9 months, and SF-36, PSQI, SIP, GAD-7, PHQ-9, IRI, Self-Compassion Scale, PACS, OCDS and recreational MDMA use at 3, 6 and 9 months; no results posted; status unknown (last update 2019).
key_findings.locator: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04158778 (API v2) › Identification; Status; Design; Outcome Measures; Eligibility

key_findings.finding: Funding and interests: the Alexander Mosley Charitable Trust funded the entire trial; sponsor Imperial College London; Awakn Life Sciences holds exclusive rights to the data; the senior author is Chief Scientific Officer of Awakn, and the first author and another author were seconded to it.
key_findings.locator: Funding; Conflict of interest; Materials and methods › Approvals and drug source, 1st paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: Two sentences are corrupted in the PMC full text: the summary of the original study's drinking results at 9 months runs from '11 participants were drinking <14' straight into unrelated words, and the age criterion reads 'aged 18 study details and finding recently undergone detoxification'. The page's HTML contains the damaged text itself (a '<' character appears to have swallowed the words between it and a later '>').
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Introduction, 2nd paragraph; Materials and methods › Procedure, 1st paragraph)
reporting_issues.consequence: The 9-month drinking figures and the age range cannot be cited from this paper; they must come from Sessa et al. (2021) or the registry (age 18 to 65).

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract and the Discussion give the success probability as 55% to 63% 'based upon either a flat or skeptical prior respectively', which pairs 55% with the flat prior; Table 1 and the Results give 0.63 for the flat prior and 0.55 for the sceptical one.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Abstract › Results; Discussion, 1st paragraph; Table 1)

reporting_issues.issue: The Beta(1,3) prior is described as a gentle distribution excluding 0% and 100% with a mean of 25%; its density is highest at 0% and falls to zero only at 100% (editors' check). It is called sceptical, but it only lowers the prior success rate in this single group; it does not express scepticism about an effect relative to any comparison.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Fig. 1 legend; Results › Bayesian analysis…, 2nd paragraph; Materials and methods › Data analysis, 2nd paragraph)
reporting_issues.consequence: The sceptical-prior result says no more than the flat one: about 9 in 14 reached the endpoint, with no comparator.

reporting_issues.issue: The paper does not say which period the baseline drinking covers; the registry describes the drinking comparison as pre-detoxification (screening) levels against later visits, and every participant had been detoxified before the course.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Materials and methods › WHO risk drinking level); registry record (Outcome Measures)
reporting_issues.consequence: If the baseline precedes detoxification, much of the two-level fall would be expected after detoxification alone; the endpoint cannot be read as an effect of the course.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says all 14 completed the course, but the questionnaire analyses at 3 months have 13 (PACS, OCDS, Self-Compassion Scale), 11 (SF-36), 14 (sleep) and 12 (IRI) participants, with no account of the missing data.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Abstract › Methods; Fig. 2 and Fig. 3 legends)
reporting_issues.consequence: Complete-case results of unknown selection; with 11 to 14 people one or two missing values can change a result.

reporting_issues.issue: The registered outcomes are change in drinking by TLFB and full questionnaires at 3, 6 and 9 months; the paper reports an unregistered endpoint (two-level WHO risk-level reduction) and its Bayesian re-expression, only the 3-month time point, and a four-item sleep score instead of the registered PSQI; registration was retrospective (first submitted January 2019, nine months after the actual start, posted November 2019).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Materials and methods › WHO risk drinking level; PROMs › Sleep); registry record (Status; Outcome Measures)
reporting_issues.consequence: Selective reporting of outcome and time point cannot be excluded.

reporting_issues.issue: The conflict-of-interest statement lists 'BS' twice among authors with no conflicts (Ben Sessa and Balázs Szigeti share the initials), and the Methods say Awakn Life Sciences has exclusive rights to the data 'from the Phase 2b', while this is a phase 1 open-label feasibility study (registry).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Conflict of interest; Materials and methods › Approvals and drug source, 1st paragraph); registry record (Design)
reporting_issues.consequence: It is unclear which author each declaration refers to and which data the commercial rights cover.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC12148347 (all sections, Table 1, figure legends, funding, conflict-of-interest and contribution statements), read in this reader's own browser tab; ClinicalTrials.gov record NCT04158778 (API v2) for registration and registered outcomes; the Crossref record for the DOI. The supplementary file (Word document, Tables S1 to S12) was not read because it is a download; Figs 1 to 3 are images and no values were taken from them.
